5404:
The word comes from Greek *synedrion*, 'sitting together', a council. Later rabbinic tradition describes a Great Sanhedrin of seventy-one members modeled on the seventy elders who assisted Moses (Num 11:16-17; Mishnah Sanhedrin 1:6), with smaller courts of twenty-three in towns. The New Testament and Josephus, closer in time, present a council of chief priests, elders and scribes convened and led by the ruling high priest (Mark 14:53; Mark 15:1; Acts 5:21). How fixed its membership and procedures were in the first century is debated; it may have been more of an advisory body summoned by the high priest than a standing court.

Under Roman rule the council handled internal religious and civil matters for Judea and controlled the temple police, who arrested Jesus and the apostles (John 18:3; Acts 5:24-26). Capital punishment, however, was reserved to the Roman governor: 'it is not lawful for us to put anyone to death' (John 18:31). Stephen's stoning appears to be a lynching rather than a lawful sentence (Acts 7:57-58), and Josephus reports that when the high priest Ananus had James the brother of Jesus stoned in AD 62, during a gap between governors, he was removed from office (*Antiquities* 20.200-203).

The gospels describe a night hearing at Caiaphas' house and a morning consultation before Jesus was handed to Pilate (Mark 14:53-65; Mark 15:1). The Mishnah's later rules forbid capital trials at night, on a festival or its eve, and require a day's delay before conviction, so some argue the proceedings were illegal; others reply that the Mishnah may describe idealized or later practice, or that the hearing was a preliminary inquiry. Not all members agreed: Nicodemus protested that the law does not judge a man without hearing him (John 7:50-51), and Joseph of Arimathea had not consented (Luke 23:50-51).

In Acts the council threatens and flogs Peter and John (Acts 4:5-21; Acts 5:27-40), where the Pharisee Gamaliel's counsel of caution prevails, tries Stephen (Acts 6:12-15), and hears Paul, who divides it by appealing to the resurrection (Acts 22:30-23:10). After AD 70 the Jerusalem Sanhedrin ceased; rabbinic courts at Yavneh and later in Galilee claimed its succession.
5407: Seventy-one members according to the Mishnah (Sanhedrin 1:6)
5411: The ruling high priest in first-century sources
5415: Jews of Jesus' day held a range of hopes for God's coming deliverance: a royal son of David, a priestly messiah, a prophet like Moses, a returning Elijah, or a heavenly Son of Man. There was no single, uniform expectation, which helps explain the debates about Jesus' identity.
5416:
'Messiah' (Hebrew *mashiach*, Greek *christos*) means 'anointed'. In the Old Testament kings were anointed (1 Sam 16:13; 1 Sam 24:6), as were priests (Lev 4:3), and Isaiah even calls the Persian Cyrus the LORD's anointed (Isa 45:1). The central messianic hope grew from God's promise to David of an everlasting dynasty (2 Sam 7:12-16). After the monarchy failed, prophets looked for a righteous branch from Jesse's stump, a ruler from Bethlehem, a restored booth of David (Isa 9:6-7; Isa 11:1-10; Jer 23:5-6; Mic 5:2; Amos 9:11).

Second Temple texts show variety. The *Psalms of Solomon* (17), written after Pompey's conquest, pray for a son of David to purge Jerusalem of Gentiles and rule in righteousness. The Qumran scrolls expect both a royal messiah of Israel and a priestly messiah of Aaron. Others waited for the prophet like Moses (Deut 18:15-18) or for Elijah before the day of the LORD (Mal 4:5-6), which is why John the Baptist was asked whether he was the Christ, Elijah or the Prophet (John 1:19-25). Daniel's 'one like a son of man' coming with the clouds to receive dominion (Dan 7:13-14) was developed in *1 Enoch* into a pre-existent heavenly judge. The suffering servant of Isaiah 52-53 was not, so far as surviving evidence shows, widely read as a dying messiah before Christianity, though this is debated.

Several would-be kings and prophets arose: after Herod's death in 4 BC men named Judas, Simon and Athronges claimed royal power; Theudas promised to part the Jordan (Acts 5:36); an Egyptian prophet led followers to the Mount of Olives (Acts 21:38). In AD 132 Simon bar Kosiba led a revolt and was hailed by Rabbi Akiva as 'Bar Kokhba', 'son of the star', alluding to Numbers 24:17. All ended in Roman defeat.

Against this background Jesus was cautious with the title. When Peter confessed him as the Christ, he spoke at once of the Son of Man suffering (Mark 8:27-33); he withdrew when crowds wanted to make him king (John 6:15); and he redefined kingship through his entry on a donkey (Zech 9:9; Matt 21:1-11) and his death. Simeon and Anna in the temple represent pious hope for the consolation and redemption of Israel (Luke 2:25-38). How the Old Testament hopes are fulfilled in Jesus, and whether some await a future earthly fulfilment for Israel, is debated among Christians.
5425: Promised before the day of the LORD (Mal 4:5)
5427: By the first century most Jews lived outside the land of Israel, in communities from Babylon to Rome. These Greek-speaking synagogues were the bridge by which the gospel reached the Gentile world.
5428:
The dispersion (Greek *diaspora*) began with the Assyrian and Babylonian deportations and grew through voluntary migration for trade and military service. Jews served as soldiers at Elephantine in Egypt under Persia, and under the Ptolemies and Seleucids large communities formed in Alexandria, Antioch and Asia Minor. Philo says Jews occupied two of Alexandria's five districts. Estimates of the total Jewish population in the first century vary widely, but most agree that more lived outside Judea than within it. The list of pilgrims at Pentecost, from Parthia and Mesopotamia to Rome, Crete and Arabia, reflects this spread (Acts 2:5-11).

Diaspora Jews kept their identity through Sabbath, circumcision, food laws, synagogues and the annual temple tax sent to Jerusalem. Julius Caesar and Augustus granted privileges: freedom to assemble, to keep the Sabbath and to send money to the temple, and exemption from military service. They read the scriptures in Greek, the Septuagint, and produced literature in Greek, including the works of Philo of Alexandria, who interpreted Moses through Platonic philosophy. Many Gentiles were attracted as 'God-fearers' who attended synagogue without full conversion (Acts 10:2; Acts 13:16), and some became proselytes (Acts 2:10; Acts 6:5).

The New Testament is full of diaspora Jews. Paul was born in Tarsus and was a Roman citizen (Acts 22:3; Acts 22:28); Barnabas was a Levite from Cyprus (Acts 4:36); Apollos was an eloquent Alexandrian (Acts 18:24); Timothy had a Jewish mother and a Greek father (Acts 16:1). Claudius expelled Jews from Rome around AD 49, which brought Priscilla and Aquila to Corinth (Acts 18:2); the Roman historian Suetonius links the expulsion to disturbances over 'Chrestus', perhaps a garbled reference to Christ. Jesus' opponents wondered if he would go to 'the dispersion among the Greeks' (John 7:35).

James and 1 Peter are addressed to the dispersion, applying the term to the church as God's scattered people (Jas 1:1; 1 Pet 1:1). Paul's mission strategy went first to the synagogue in each city (Acts 13:5; Acts 14:1), and the tension over Gentile inclusion without circumcision was largely a diaspora question. Esther and Daniel had already shown faithful Jews living in a foreign empire (Esth 4:14; Dan 6:10).
5431: Jews occupied two of five districts, according to Philo
5435: Assembly, Sabbath, temple tax, exemption from military service
5439: The religious world of Paul's churches was crowded with civic gods, household spirits, healing shrines, oracles, magic and initiatory 'mystery' cults. Conversion to Christ meant leaving much of this daily practice behind.
5440:
Greek and Roman religion was civic and practical rather than creedal. Each city honored its gods with temples, festivals, processions and sacrifices, on the principle of reciprocity, 'I give so that you may give'. Priests were often civic officials, and piety meant performing rites correctly rather than holding particular beliefs. Households honored their own protective spirits, the Roman *lares* and *penates*, at small shrines. Because sacrifice was woven into guild banquets, civic festivals and the meat market, Christians in Corinth had to ask whether they could eat food offered to idols (1 Cor 8:1-13; 1 Cor 10:14-30).

Acts shows this world vividly. At Lystra the crowd hails Barnabas as Zeus and Paul as Hermes, recalling a local legend of the gods visiting in human form, and the priest of Zeus brings oxen to sacrifice (Acts 14:8-18). In Athens Paul finds an altar 'to an unknown god' (Acts 17:23). At Ephesus, home of the great temple of Artemis, one of the seven wonders of the world, silversmiths riot when the gospel threatens their trade in shrines (Acts 19:23-41), and new believers burn magic books worth 50,000 silver drachmas (Acts 19:19). A slave girl at Philippi has a 'python spirit', linked with the Delphic oracle (Acts 16:16-18), and Paul's last ship bears the figurehead of the Twin Brothers, Castor and Pollux, protectors of sailors (Acts 28:11). Healing shrines of Asclepius, such as those at Corinth and Pergamum, drew the sick.

The mystery religions offered something more personal: secret initiation into the story of a deity, promising blessing in this life and a better lot after death. The oldest were the Eleusinian mysteries of Demeter and Persephone near Athens. Others honored Dionysus, Isis and Osiris (described in Apuleius' *Metamorphoses* book 11), and Cybele and Attis. The cult of Mithras as practised in the Roman army flourished mostly from the late first century to the fourth. Their rites were secret, so much of what we know is fragmentary and late.

In the early twentieth century the 'history of religions' school argued that Paul's teaching on baptism and the Lord's Supper borrowed from these cults' dying-and-rising gods and sacred meals. Critics point out that most evidence for the cults' parallels dates after the New Testament, that the myths are seasonal rather than historical, and that Paul's language is rooted in Jewish categories such as Passover and covenant (1 Cor 5:7; 1 Cor 11:23-26). Most scholars now see shared vocabulary rather than borrowing, though the conversation continues. Paul's warning against sharing the table of the Lord and the table of demons (1 Cor 10:20-21) shows that he saw the two as rivals, not cousins.

5446: Rites of Demeter and Persephone near Athens
5448: Roman form flourished c. late 1st to 4th century AD

5452: Across the Roman East, cities honored the emperor with temples, priests, sacrifices and festivals as a divine savior and lord. Christian confession of Jesus as Lord and Son of God sounded, in this setting, like a rival allegiance.
5453:
After Julius Caesar was officially deified in 42 BC, his adopted son Octavian, later Augustus, took the title *divi filius*, 'son of the divine one'. In Rome emperors were usually deified only after death, but in the Greek East living emperors received worship as gods from the start: Augustus permitted temples to Rome and himself at Pergamum and Nicomedia in 29 BC. Emperor worship was promoted not mainly by emperors but by provincial elites eager to show loyalty, and it was woven into civic life through festivals, games, statues and oaths.

The language of this cult overlapped with the gospel's. A famous inscription from Priene (9 BC), adopting Augustus' birthday as the start of the provincial year, praises him as a savior who ended war and says his birthday was the beginning of 'good news' (*euangelia*) for the world. Emperors were called savior (*soter*), lord (*kyrios*), and son of god. Against this backdrop, Paul's proclamation of Jesus as Lord, before whom every knee will bow, and of a Savior from heaven (Phil 2:9-11; Phil 3:20), and the charge at Thessalonica that Christians said 'there is another king, Jesus' (Acts 17:7), carried political force. Some scholars argue Paul deliberately countered imperial ideology; others think the overlap is less intentional.

In the province of Asia, cities competed to be 'temple-keepers' (*neokoroi*) of the emperor's cult: Pergamum, with its early temple to Augustus; Smyrna, awarded a temple to Tiberius in AD 26; and Ephesus, which built a temple of the Flavian emperors around AD 89/90 under Domitian. These are among the seven churches of Revelation (Rev 2:1-17). 'Satan's throne' at Pergamum (Rev 2:13) may refer to the imperial cult, and Revelation's beast that demands worship of its image and controls buying and selling (Rev 13:4-17) is widely read against emperor worship.

Early in the second century Pliny the Younger, governor of Bithynia, tested accused Christians by asking them to offer incense and wine to the emperor's image and curse Christ, executing those who refused (*Letters* 10.96). The account of Polycarp's martyrdom has the magistrate urging him to say 'Caesar is Lord'. Thomas' confession 'my Lord and my God' (John 20:28) and the Christian refusal to offer even a pinch of incense show how exclusive confession of Christ collided with imperial religion.

5465: Stoics and Epicureans were the two most influential philosophical schools of the New Testament era, offering rival accounts of the gods, the world and the good life. Paul met both in Athens, and their vocabulary echoes in the letters.
5466:
Stoicism was founded by Zeno of Citium, who taught at the Painted Stoa in Athens around 300 BC. Stoics held that the universe is a single rational whole pervaded by divine reason (*logos*), sometimes called Zeus or God or Nature. The wise person lives 'according to nature', regards virtue as the only true good, and is indifferent to wealth, health and status, achieving freedom from destructive passions. Stoics believed in providence and a cyclical conflagration and renewal of the cosmos. In Paul's time leading Stoics included Seneca, Nero's tutor and the brother of Gallio, proconsul of Achaia (Acts 18:12-17), and slightly later Epictetus, a former slave whose *Discourses* were recorded by a student.

Epicureanism was founded by Epicurus (341-270 BC), who taught in his Garden at Athens. The world is made of atoms moving in a void; the gods exist but live in blissful detachment and do not intervene; the soul dissolves at death, so 'death is nothing to us'. The goal of life is pleasure, understood as tranquillity (*ataraxia*) and absence of pain, best found in simple living and friendship. The Roman poet Lucretius set out the system in *On the Nature of Things*. Opponents caricatured it as 'eat, drink and be merry', and Paul quotes Isaiah's version of that motto against those who deny resurrection (1 Cor 15:32; Isa 22:13).

In Athens Epicurean and Stoic philosophers debated with Paul and brought him to the Areopagus (Acts 17:18-19). His speech engages both: against Epicureans, God made the world and is near to every person; with Stoics, God needs nothing and gives life and breath; he quotes 'we are his offspring', from the Stoic-influenced poet Aratus (Acts 17:24-28). But his call to repentance before a fixed day of judgment by a man raised from the dead offended both schools (Acts 17:30-32).

Scholars note Stoic echoes elsewhere: Paul's contentment (*autarkes*, a Stoic ideal) in all circumstances, grounded in Christ's strength rather than self-sufficiency (Phil 4:11-13); the role of conscience (Rom 2:14-15); and lists of virtues and vices (Gal 5:19-23). John's *logos* (John 1:1-14) has been linked to Stoic and to Philo's usage, though most see its primary roots in the Old Testament word and wisdom of God (Gen 1:3; Ps 33:6; Prov 8:22-31). How far biblical writers borrowed from philosophy, and how far they confronted it, is part of the wider question of revelation and culture.
5468: Zeno of Citium, Athens, c. 300 BC

5480: Roman roads, sea lanes and a century of relative peace made travel easier than ever before, though it remained slow, costly and dangerous. Knowing typical distances and speeds brings biblical journeys down to earth.
5481:
Rome built a network of some 80,000 km of main paved roads, with milestones every Roman mile (about 1,480 m). In Paul's world the Via Egnatia, built in the second century BC, ran across Macedonia through Philippi, Amphipolis, Apollonia and Thessalonica, exactly the route of Acts 17:1. The Via Appia brought Paul to Rome, where believers met him at the Forum of Appius and Three Taverns (Acts 28:15). The imperial courier service could average around 75 km a day using relays of horses, but ordinary people walked. A traveler on foot typically covered 25-30 km (15-20 miles) a day; a loaded donkey or caravan moved at about the same pace or slower.

Sea travel was faster with a fair wind and could cover 100-150 km a day, but it was seasonal. Sailing was considered dangerous from mid-September and largely suspended from about November to March; Paul's voyage was risky because 'the Fast', the Day of Atonement, was already past (Acts 27:9). Alexandrian grain ships, large enough to carry 276 people (Acts 27:37), could reach Rome in two to three weeks but took much longer on the return against prevailing winds. Travelers faced shipwreck, bandits, rivers and exposure, as Paul's catalogue of dangers shows (2 Cor 11:25-27), and stayed with hosts or in inns of poor reputation (Luke 10:34).

Some biblical travel times, using these rates: Ezra's party took about four months to travel from Babylon to Jerusalem, leaving on the first day of the first month and arriving on the first day of the fifth (Ezra 7:8-9). Deuteronomy notes it is eleven days from Horeb to Kadesh-barnea by the Mount Seir road (Deut 1:2). Nazareth to Bethlehem is about 150 km, perhaps four to seven days for Mary and Joseph (Luke 2:4-5). Galilee to Jerusalem was roughly 120-150 km, three to five days, by the Jordan valley route or directly through Samaria (Luke 9:51-53; John 4:3-4). Jerusalem to Jericho is about 27 km with a descent of roughly 1,000 m, the steep, lonely road of the good Samaritan (Luke 10:30). Emmaus was 60 stadia, about 11 km, from Jerusalem (Luke 24:13), and a Sabbath day's journey about 1 km (Acts 1:12).

Paul's journeys, adding land and sea, are often estimated at well over 10,000 km, though such figures depend on reconstructing his routes. His letters were carried by co-workers such as Phoebe, Tychicus and Epaphroditus (Rom 16:1-2; Col 4:7-8; Phil 2:25), and churches sent people back and forth with news and gifts, creating a network that made a scattered movement feel like one body.

5497: Most people ate a simple diet built on bread, olive oil and wine, with vegetables, legumes, fruit and occasional fish or meat. Meals were also social events that marked status and belonging, which is why Jesus' table fellowship mattered so much.
5498:
The Mediterranean staples were grain, new wine and oil (Deut 7:13; Ps 104:14-15). Bread supplied perhaps half or more of an ordinary person's calories, so 'daily bread' was no metaphor (Matt 6:11). Wheat bread was preferred; barley was cheaper and associated with the poor, as with the boy's five barley loaves (John 6:9). Revelation's famine price, a quart of wheat for a denarius or three of barley, implies roughly a day's wage for one person's daily bread (Rev 6:6). Women ground grain each day by hand mill (Matt 24:41) and baked in household or shared ovens.

Alongside bread came lentils and beans (Gen 25:34; Ezek 4:9), onions, leeks and garlic (Num 11:5), olives, figs, grapes, dates and pomegranates, cheese, curds and honey. Around the Sea of Galilee fish were dried or salted for trade; Magdala's Greek name, Taricheae, probably refers to fish-salting. Meat was costly and reserved for festivals, sacrifices and guests, which is why killing the fatted calf signalled extravagant celebration (Luke 15:23). Wine was the normal drink, usually diluted with water, and John the Baptist's diet of locusts and wild honey marked him as a wilderness figure (Mark 1:6).

Ordinary people ate a light morning meal and a main meal in the evening. At formal dinners, following Greco-Roman custom, guests reclined on couches around low tables, leaning on the left elbow with feet extended away from the table. This explains how a woman could stand behind Jesus at his feet and wash them (Luke 7:37-38) and how the beloved disciple could lean back against Jesus' chest (John 13:23-25). Places reflected rank (Luke 14:7-11), and the host's choice of guests displayed his social circle (Luke 14:12-14).

Because eating together signalled acceptance, Jesus' meals with tax collectors and sinners drew criticism (Mark 2:15-17; Luke 15:1-2), and table fellowship between Jews and Gentiles became the crisis at Antioch (Gal 2:11-14). Early Christians ate the Lord's Supper as part of a full meal in homes, and Paul rebukes the Corinthians because wealthier members ate and drank while poorer ones went hungry (1 Cor 11:17-34). Scripture's hope is pictured as a feast: rich food and aged wine on God's mountain, many coming from east and west to recline with Abraham, and the marriage supper of the Lamb (Isa 25:6-8; Matt 8:11; Rev 19:9).

5510: Most biblical-era families lived in small stone or mud-brick houses grouped around shared courtyards, with flat roofs used as living space. Clothing was simple, a tunic and a cloak, and many laws and sayings assume its details.
